## Build: Lists

```{webr-r}
# A list can hold mixed, differently-shaped things together
sample_info <- list(
  id = "GSM3119015",
  values = c(12, 18, 9),
  notes = "control group"
)
sample_info$notes
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## ⚪ About This — Why Lists?
A data frame requires every column to be the same length. A list doesn't — 
it's the structure R reaches for when things genuinely don't fit a tidy 
rectangle, which happens more often than you'd expect once you start working 
with real analysis output (model results, nested settings, mixed metadata).
:::

## Build: Base R Subsetting (Just Enough to Read Code)

```{webr-r}
rawc[1, ]              # entire first row
rawc[, 3]              # entire third column
rawc[1059, "GSM3119015"]   # one specific cell
rawc$GSM3119015             # a column, by name
```

Conditional subsetting uses the same comparison operators you already know:
`==`, `!=`, `>`, `<`, `>=`, `<=`, and `%in%`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## 🔍 Learn More — You Don't Need to Master This Today
There are several equally valid ways to subset in base R. The goal here is 
recognition, not fluency — so that when you see `df[row, col]` or `df$col` 
in someone else's script, you're not stopped cold.
:::

## Build: Checking for Missing Values

```{webr-r}
anyNA(rawc)
which(is.na(rawc$GSM3119015))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## 🔍 Learn More — Zero vs. NA: Not the Same Thing
A `0` means "we measured this, and the value was zero." An `NA` means 
"we don't know this value." Replacing a missing value with `0` without 
thinking it through can quietly distort every downstream calculation — 
averages, totals, and models all treat a fabricated zero as real data.
:::

## Build: Writing Your Own Function

```{webr-r}
celsius_to_fahrenheit <- function(temp_c) {
  temp_f <- (temp_c * 9/5) + 32
  return(temp_f)
}
celsius_to_fahrenheit(20)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## ⚪ About This — Why Write a Function?
This is the **DRY principle** — Don't Repeat Yourself. If you find yourself 
copy-pasting the same calculation more than twice, that's the signal to 
wrap it in a function instead.
:::

## Build: `for` Loops

```{webr-r}
for (i in 1:5) {
  print(i^2)
}
```

## Build: `if` / `else` Conditionals

```{webr-r}
check_value <- function(x) {
  if (x > 0) {
    "positive"
  } else if (x < 0) {
    "negative"
  } else {
    "zero"
  }
}
check_value(-4)
```

## Build: Reading an Error Message (Deliberate Exercise)

```{r}
#| eval: false
mean(FamAges)   # object doesn't exist yet — intentional
```

::: {.callout-important collapse="true"}
## 🔴 Instructor Note
Let this error sit uncorrected for a beat before explaining. The goal is 
normalizing errors as information, not something to panic over — most of 
your future debugging time will be spent reading messages like this one.
:::

## What We Did, and Why

**What we built:** lists, base R subsetting, a custom function, a `for` 
loop, an `if`/`else` conditional, and a deliberate error.

**Why it matters:** these are the building blocks that let a script adapt 
to real data instead of breaking the first time something doesn't match 
exactly what you expected.
